full_judgment:
2. Facts giving rise to the proceeding are as follows: A conditional agreement was reached between the employers and employees vide annexure A which was subject to the approval of the Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation (hereinafter referred to as BIMC). In the said agreement subject to the approval of BJMC, certain benefits were given to the workers. The BJMC however, vide its circular dated 28-3-73, directed the Manager of Sonali Jute Mills to stop immediately the additional benefits and also directed to realize excess which were already made by way of deducting from the pay vide annexure C&D of the petition. Accordingly, circular was issued be the employer that since BJMC has not given the consent the additional benefits as was agreed to between the parties earlier could not be available and further informed that the payment which has already been made in excess will be deducted from the workers wages. Thereafter, the workers union had filed a proceedings and also prayed for an order of injunction under or. 39, rule 1 and 2 C.P.C. The employer by filing written statement objected to the prayer and, inter alia, mentioned that finding no other alternative and also to keep the good relationship with the worker it was forced to sign 2 provisional agreements on 2-1-72 and 7-6-73 whereby certain additional financial benefits was given to the Sardars and Mistries of the Mechanical Department but this agreement was absolutely subject to final approval of the BJMC. It was also pointed out that the workers union had agreed to refund the additional money in case BJMC disapproved of such payment. Now BJMC has disapproved the agreement in question and instructed to stop the additional payment as per provisional agreement and also directed to realize the additional amount that was already paid. The employer had to do so and the Court should not grant any injunction because that would mean payment of few lacs of taka to the workers and prayed for vacating the ad-interim order that was granted by the Court on 25-7-73. The learned Labor Court on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case came to the conclusion that the workers union, the first party, would suffer irreparable loss if the temporary injunction is not granted and also noticed the contention of the 2nd party that order of injunction under Order 39, rule 1 C.P.C. may not be granted. The learned Labor Court found that there was substance in the contention but concluded that section 151 C.P.C. could be invoked to give the relief and accordingly issued the injunction restraining the 2nd partly from stopping the benefit granted to the 1st party on the basis of the agreement dated 25-7-73. 

 1) That the agreement was absolutely provisional which again was subject to approval of the BJMC and as such the same was no settlement within the meaning of Industrial Relations Ordinance. Secondly, whether the Labor Court had the power of granting injunction under Order 39, rule 1 and 2 C.P.C. 

 4. Mr. Asrarul Hossain contended that by adding a fiction of law by the expression "deemed" the Labor Court has been given of necessity the powers of enforcing attendance of a person and witnesses, compelling the production of documents, etc. and issuing commissions for examination of witnesses, etc. solely for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute. "Industrial Dispute" has been defined in section 2 clause (xiii) which means "any dispute or difference between employers and employers or between employers and workmen or between workmen and workmen which is connected with the employment or non-employment or the terms of employments or the conditions of work of any person." Section 43 postulates that no industrial dispute shall be deemed to exist unless it has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent. In other words, the law does not recognize the existence of industrial dispute unless it is raised by a collective bargaining agent in the prescribed manner, namely by negotiation (section 26), conciliation (section 29), arbitration (section 31) and adjudication by Labor Court (section 35). Present dispute was not raised as an industrial dispute and as such it cannot be termed as industrial dispute within the meaning of enactment. Nor the present agreement could be called settlement because settlement has been defined in clause (xxiv) of sec. 2 which provides, amongst others, "such agreement is in writing, has been signed by the parties thereto in such manner as may be prescribed and a copy thereof has been sent to Provincial Government the Conciliator and such other person as may be prescribed". In this view of the matter the exercise of the jurisdiction of the Labor Court under section 36 was unwarranted inasmuch as it was not exercising the jurisdiction for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute. The next question whether the power of injunction was conferred on it must be answered in the negative because it was also deemed to be a Civil Court for limited purpose. In the case of Bangladesh Fishermen's Co operative Society Ltd. Vs. The Chairman, Labor Court, Chittagong and Mr. Bashir Ahmed (1975) 27 D.L.R. 367 the same view was expressed by a Division Bench of this Court where it was observed the use of the word "deemed" in this case definitely indicates that a Labor Court is not ordinarily a Civil Court but it shall be considered to be so in respect of the proceedings before it for deciding an industrial dispute but not for all purposes. It merely means it shall have all the powers of civil Court for regulating the procedure in respect of such a proceedings. The same view was expressed in the case of Khulna Tobacco Vs. Chairman, Labor Court (1977) 29 D.L.R. 148. Thus it is clear that the consensus judicial opinion is that the Labor Court is a Civil Court for limited purpose and since the power of injunction has not been conferred on it the canons of interpretation suggests that such power is not available because the power must be conferred expressly. In this view of the matter the opinion that the power of issuing injunction by the Labor Court was not available because the relevant enactment has not conferred it. 

 5. In the result, therefore, this Rule must be made absolute and the opinion is the agreement was neither a settlement nor the dispute was industrial dispute within the meaning of Industrial Relations Ordinance and as such exercise of jurisdiction under section 36 of the Labor Court was not called upon because it was not "for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute."
